1.0The method1.NNotes1.1.1Two sine sources, resistors only → e₂(t) (AUT24 · Q1(a))1.1.2Two unknown nodes (R–2R ladder) (AUT23 · Q1(b))1.1.3Current source into a node (AUT22 · Q1(b))1.1.4Unbalanced bridge — current through R₅ (AUT25 · Q1(a))

1.0The method

Do this for every question in the section.

1.0.1The one method: KCL at every unknown node

Every DC question in this section can be done with this. Dividers and Millman are only shortcuts.

  1. Pick a ground. If none is drawn, use the node the question measures from (e.g. node 4 for V24), or the bottom wire.
  2. List every node and cross off the known ones. Ground = 0 V. The top of a voltage source whose bottom is on ground = that source's voltage.
  3. Count what's left. A node that only touches resistors (and current sources) is unknown. One unknown → one equation. Two → two.
  4. KCL at each unknown node: every current written as leaving, all added up = 0. Write my node first.
  5. Solve. Multiply through to clear fractions, or use the calculator's simultaneous-equation mode.
  6. Answer what was asked: a voltage between two nodes = ea − eb; a current = Ohm's law on that resistor.
eme−eotherR(current leaving through each resistor)\frac{e_{\text{me}} - e_{\text{other}}}{R} \quad\text{(current leaving through each resistor)}Reme​−eother​​(current leaving through each resistor)
∑currents leaving=0\sum \text{currents leaving} = 0∑currents leaving=0

1.0.2Why the currents add to zero

Charge can't pile up at a point: what flows in must flow out. If every arrow is drawn leaving, a current that really flows in just comes out negative, so the total is 0.

(−2 mA)+(+2 mA)=0(-2\ \text{mA}) + (+2\ \text{mA}) = 0(−2 mA)+(+2 mA)=0

1.0.3Current sources

A current source fixes the current, not the voltage. Put its value straight into the KCL sum.

  • Arrow into the node → minus (it is −I leaving).
  • Arrow out of the node → plus.
  • A resistor in series with a current source never appears: the current is the same whatever its value.

1.0.4Shortcut: when a divider is enough

One single loop (everything in series) → the voltage divider gives the answer straight away:

V2=Vs R2R1+R2V_2 = V_s\,\frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}V2​=Vs​R1​+R2​R2​​

A resistor joining two "middle" nodes (a bridge) → no divider. Use KCL at both.

1.0.5Before you write the answer

  • Units in seconds for t: 1.25 ms = 1.25 × 10−3 s.
  • Calculator in RAD mode for sin/cos.
  • Give a number and a unit, 3 significant figures.
Mkmµnp

1.NNotes

Ohm's law & power

V=IRV = IRV=IR
P=VI=I2R=V2RP = VI = I^2R = \frac{V^2}{R}P=VI=I2R=RV2​
  • Current entering the + terminal → element absorbs P = VI. Resistors always absorb.

Series & parallel

Rs=R1+R2R_s = R_1 + R_2Rs​=R1​+R2​
R1∥R2=R1R2R1+R2R_1 \parallel R_2 = \frac{R_1R_2}{R_1+R_2}R1​∥R2​=R1​+R2​R1​R2​​
  • Series = same current. Parallel = same two nodes.
  • Parallel is always smaller than the smallest one.

Dividers

V2=Vs R2R1+R2V_2 = V_s\,\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}V2​=Vs​R1​+R2​R2​​
I1=I R2R1+R2I_1 = I\,\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}I1​=IR1​+R2​R2​​
  • Voltage divider: own resistor on top. Current divider: other resistor on top.

Sources

  • Voltage source fixes the voltage; current source fixes the current (arrow direction).
  • Resistor in series with a current source doesn't change the current.
  • Open terminal → no current → no drop.

Nodal analysis (KCL)

∑en−eneighbourR=Iinjected\sum \frac{e_n - e_{\text{neighbour}}}{R} = I_{\text{injected}}∑Ren​−eneighbour​​=Iinjected​
e=∑Vk/Rk∑1/Rke = \frac{\sum V_k/R_k}{\sum 1/R_k}e=∑1/Rk​∑Vk​/Rk​​
  • Second formula (Millman): shortcut for one unknown node.
  • Voltage source to ground fixes that node. Source between two nodes → supernode + ea − eb = V.

Superposition

e(t)=k1V1(t)+k2V2(t)e(t) = k_1V_1(t) + k_2V_2(t)e(t)=k1​V1​(t)+k2​V2​(t)
  • One source at a time: V source → short, I source → open.
  • Resistors only → same sine out, just scaled.

Thévenin & controlled sources

Vth=Vopen circuitV_{th} = V_{\text{open circuit}}Vth​=Vopen circuit​
Rth=VtItR_{th} = \frac{V_t}{I_t}Rth​=It​Vt​​
  • Rth: switch off independent sources (V → short, I → open).
  • Never switch off a controlled source: use a test source.

1.1Worked examples

Exam values. Each one: what's new, the paper as printed, then the full solution.
Problem 1.1.1 (AUT24 · Q1(a), 20%). Two sine sources, resistors only → e₂(t).
What's new here
  • Nodes 1 and 3 sit on sources, so they are known. Only node 2 is unknown → one KCL equation.
  • Resistors only, so each sine just gets scaled. The answer is a·sin + b·cos.
  • t in seconds, calculator in RAD.
Solution.
1.

KCL at node 2 (works at every instant)

e2−V1R1+e2R2+e2−V2R3=0\frac{e_2 - V_1}{R_1} + \frac{e_2}{R_2} + \frac{e_2 - V_2}{R_3} = 0R1​e2​−V1​​+R2​e2​​+R3​e2​−V2​​=0
e2=1/R11/R1+1/R2+1/R3⏟k1=0.5238V1+1/R31/R1+1/R2+1/R3⏟k2=0.1905V2e_2 = \underbrace{\frac{1/R_1}{1/R_1+1/R_2+1/R_3}}_{k_1 = 0.5238}V_1 + \underbrace{\frac{1/R_3}{1/R_1+1/R_2+1/R_3}}_{k_2 = 0.1905}V_2e2​=k1​=0.52381/R1​+1/R2​+1/R3​1/R1​​​​V1​+k2​=0.19051/R1​+1/R2​+1/R3​1/R3​​​​V2​
2.

Paste in the sources

e2(t)=0.5238×5.00sin⁡(2000πt)+0.1905×2.00cos⁡(5000πt)e_2(t) = 0.5238\times 5.00\sin(2000\pi t) + 0.1905\times2.00\cos(5000\pi t)e2​(t)=0.5238×5.00sin(2000πt)+0.1905×2.00cos(5000πt)
e2(t)=2.62sin⁡(2000πt)+0.381cos⁡(5000πt) V\boxed{e_2(t) = 2.62\sin(2000\pi t) + 0.381\cos(5000\pi t)\ \text{V}}e2​(t)=2.62sin(2000πt)+0.381cos(5000πt) V​
3.

Evaluate at t = 1.25 ms

sin⁡(2000π×1.25m)=1.00,cos⁡(5000π×1.25m)=0.707\sin(2000\pi\times1.25\text{m}) = 1.00, \qquad \cos(5000\pi\times1.25\text{m}) = 0.707sin(2000π×1.25m)=1.00,cos(5000π×1.25m)=0.707
e2=2.62(1.00)+0.381(0.707)=2.89 Ve_2 = 2.62(1.00) + 0.381(0.707) = \boxed{2.89\,\mathrm{V}}e2​=2.62(1.00)+0.381(0.707)=2.89V​
Trap Set the calculator to radians. 2000π×1.25 ms = 2.5π, not 2.5°.
Why it works No capacitors or inductors means the output is just a weighted sum of the inputs (superposition). AUT24 asked for e2, SPR25 asked for i1 on the same circuit.
Answer.sin coefficient (V) = 2.62 V  ·  cos coefficient (V) = 381 mV  ·  e2(t0) = 2.89 V
Problem 1.1.2 (AUT23 · Q1(b), 20%). Two unknown nodes (R–2R ladder).
What's new here
  • Nodes 1 and 2 only touch resistors → two unknowns, two KCL equations.
  • A resistor above a source: its far end sits at the source voltage (1 V here).
  • Multiply each equation by 2000 to clear the fractions, then substitute.
Solution.
1.

KCL at node 1

e1−Vb1R3+e1−e2R1=0\frac{e_1 - V_{b1}}{R_3} + \frac{e_1 - e_2}{R_1} = 0R3​e1​−Vb1​​+R1​e1​−e2​​=0
2.

KCL at node 2

e2−e1R1+e2−Vb0R4+e2R2=0\frac{e_2 - e_1}{R_1} + \frac{e_2 - V_{b0}}{R_4} + \frac{e_2}{R_2} = 0R1​e2​−e1​​+R4​e2​−Vb0​​+R2​e2​​=0
3.

Matrix form (conductances in mS, kΩ units → mA)

[1.500−1.000−1.0002.000][e1e2]=[0.50000.5000]\begin{bmatrix} 1.500 & -1.000 \\ -1.000 & 2.000 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} e_1 \\ e_2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.5000 \\ 0.5000 \end{bmatrix}[1.500−1.000​−1.0002.000​][e1​e2​​]=[0.50000.5000​]
4.

Solve (Cramer's rule)

Δ=1.500×2.000−(−1.000)2=2.000\Delta = 1.500\times2.000 - (-1.000)^2 = 2.000Δ=1.500×2.000−(−1.000)2=2.000
e1=0.5000×2.000−(−1.000)(0.5000)Δ=750 mVe_1 = \frac{0.5000\times2.000 - (-1.000)(0.5000)}{\Delta} = \boxed{750\,\mathrm{mV}}e1​=Δ0.5000×2.000−(−1.000)(0.5000)​=750mV​
e2=1.500×0.5000−(−1.000)(0.5000)Δ=625 mVe_2 = \frac{1.500\times0.5000 - (-1.000)(0.5000)}{\Delta} = 625\,\mathrm{mV}e2​=Δ1.500×0.5000−(−1.000)(0.5000)​=625mV
Why it works Working in kΩ and mA keeps numbers small: 1/1 kΩ = 1 mS. AUT23 asked for e1, SPR24 asked for e2 of the same circuit — solve both every time.
Answer.e1 = 750 mV
Problem 1.1.3 (AUT22 · Q1(b), 20%). Current source into a node.
What's new here
  • No ground drawn: pick node 4 (the question measures V24 from it), so V24 = e2.
  • Current source: its arrow points into node 2, so it enters KCL as −I4.
  • R5 never appears: it is in series with the current source.
Solution.
1.

Ground node 4, read the arrow

Arrow points left → I4 is pulled out of node 3 and pushed into node 2.

R5 is in series with I4, so it carries exactly I4 no matter its value. It cannot affect node 2.

2.

KCL at node 2 (out = in)

e2−V1R2+e2R3=I4\frac{e_2 - V_1}{R_2} + \frac{e_2}{R_3} = I_4R2​e2​−V1​​+R3​e2​​=I4​
e2=V1R2+I41R2+1R3=1.0002000+0.000500012000+13000=1.20 Ve_2 = \frac{\dfrac{V_1}{R_2} + I_4}{\dfrac{1}{R_2}+\dfrac{1}{R_3}} = \frac{\dfrac{1.000}{2000} + 0.0005000}{\dfrac{1}{2000}+\dfrac{1}{3000}} = 1.20\,\mathrm{V}e2​=R2​1​+R3​1​R2​V1​​+I4​​=20001​+30001​20001.000​+0.0005000​=1.20V
3.

Answer

V24=e2−e4=1.20 VV_{24} = e_2 - e_4 = \boxed{1.20\,\mathrm{V}}V24​=e2​−e4​=1.20V​
Trap R5 is a decoy. A resistor in series with a current source never changes that branch's current.
Why it works AUT22 asked V24, SPR23 asked V12 — same circuit, same e2.
Answer.V24 = 1.20 V
Problem 1.1.4 (AUT25 · Q1(a), 20%). Unbalanced bridge — current through R₅.
What's new here
  • No ground drawn: bottom wire = 0 V, top wire = Vs.
  • R5 joins A and B, so dividers don't work. Two unknowns → KCL at A and at B.
  • Messy numbers: use simultaneous mode in kΩ, then I = (eA − eB)/R5.
Solution.
1.

Remove R5: two plain dividers

VA=VsR2R1+R2=5.82 V,VB=VsR4R3+R4=5.29 VV_A = V_s\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2} = 5.82\,\mathrm{V}, \qquad V_B = V_s\frac{R_4}{R_3+R_4} = 5.29\,\mathrm{V}VA​=Vs​R1​+R2​R2​​=5.82V,VB​=Vs​R3​+R4​R4​​=5.29V
Vth=VA−VB=536 mVV_{th} = V_A - V_B = 536\,\mathrm{mV}Vth​=VA​−VB​=536mV
2.

Kill Vs (short it) → Rth

With Vs shorted, the top and bottom rails are one node. From A: R1∥R2 to that node, then R3∥R4 to B — exactly HW 0 Q1(d).

Rth=R1∥R2+R3∥R4=776 Ω+1.94 kΩ=2.72 kΩR_{th} = R_1\parallel R_2 + R_3\parallel R_4 = 776\,\Omega + 1.94\,\mathrm{k}\Omega = 2.72\,\mathrm{k}\OmegaRth​=R1​∥R2​+R3​∥R4​=776Ω+1.94kΩ=2.72kΩ
3.

Put R5 back

I(R5)=VthRth+R5=536 mV2.72 kΩ+5600 Ω=64.5 μAI(R_5) = \frac{V_{th}}{R_{th}+R_5} = \frac{536\,\mathrm{mV}}{2.72\,\mathrm{k}\Omega + 5600\,\Omega} = \boxed{64.5\,\mu\mathrm{A}}I(R5​)=Rth​+R5​Vth​​=2.72kΩ+5600Ω536mV​=64.5μA​
Why it works Nodal analysis (two equations at A and B) gives the same answer. Thévenin is faster here because each piece is a skill you already have.
Answer.I(R5) = 64.5 µA
eeen20020 · lock-in notesSection 2

2First-order transients

RC and RL circuits after a switch or a step · Q1(b) or Q1(c) in every paper · Q3 in AUT25
contents
2.0The method2.NNotes2.1.1RC step up → capacitor voltage (AUT22 · Q1(c))2.1.2RL step from a non-zero start → node voltage (AUT23 · Q1(c))2.1.3Switch closes, inductor in parallel with a resistor (SPR21 · Q1(c))2.1.4Voltage pulse into RL → node voltage (sign trap) (SPR25 · Q1(b))2.1.5Square wave into RC: steady-state max and min (AUT25 · Q3)

2.0The method

Do this for every question in the section.

2.0.1One formula for every question

One capacitor or one inductor: the answer slides from a start value to a final value.

x(t)=x∞+(x0−x∞) e−(t−t0)/τx(t) = x_{\infty} + (x_0 - x_{\infty})\,e^{-(t - t_0)/\tau}x(t)=x∞​+(x0​−x∞​)e−(t−t0​)/τ
x0start value, just before the switch
x∞final value, long after the switch
τtime constant
t0when the switch happens
  1. Start value (old circuit, L = wire, C = gap).
  2. Final value (new circuit, L = wire, C = gap).
  3. τ from the resistance L or C sees.
  4. Put them in the formula.

2.0.2Start value

  • Inductor current can't jump. Capacitor voltage can't jump.
  • "For a long time" = steady state: L = wire, C = gap. Solve that DC circuit.
  • If the question asks for a node voltage, find the L current or C voltage first, then get the node voltage from it.

2.0.3Final value

Same idea with the new source value: L = wire, C = gap, solve the DC circuit.

  • One loop left → voltage divider (or KCL, same answer).
  • A node with three or more branches → KCL.

2.0.4Time constant

τ=RCτ=LR\tau = RC \qquad\qquad \tau = \frac{L}{R}τ=RCτ=RL​

R = the resistance the L or C sees between its two ends with the sources off: V source → short, I source → open.

Series → add. Both from the same node to ground → parallel.

2.0.5Pulses: two stages

  1. Stage 1: the normal formula, up to the end of the pulse.
  2. The answer from stage 1 becomes the start of stage 2.
  3. Stage 2: the normal formula again, heading to 0.

τ is the same in both stages: only the source changes, not the circuit.

2.0.6Before you write the answer

  • Use t − t0, the time since the switch.
  • µ = 10−6, m = 10−3. Same prefix top and bottom in t/τ.
  • After 1τ: 63% of the way. After 5τ: finished.
  • Number and unit, 3 significant figures.

2.NNotes

The formula

x(t)=x∞+(x0−x∞) e−(t−t0)/τx(t) = x_{\infty} + (x_0 - x_{\infty})\,e^{-(t - t_0)/\tau}x(t)=x∞​+(x0​−x∞​)e−(t−t0​)/τ
  • 1τ → 63% of the way. 5τ → finished.

Time constant

τ=RC\tau = RCτ=RC
τ=LR\tau = \frac{L}{R}τ=RL​
  • R seen by L or C with sources off (V → short, I → open).

Steady state

  • Inductor = wire.
  • Capacitor = gap (open circuit).

Can't jump

  • Inductor current.
  • Capacitor voltage.
  • Everything else can jump at the switch.

Charging and decaying

x=x∞(1−e−t/τ)x = x_{\infty}\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right)x=x∞​(1−e−t/τ)
x=x0 e−t/τx = x_0\,e^{-t/\tau}x=x0​e−t/τ
  • First: starting from 0. Second: heading to 0.

Square wave, steady state

Vmax=VH+(Vmin−VH) e−T/2τV_{max} = V_H + (V_{min} - V_H)\,e^{-T/2\tau}Vmax​=VH​+(Vmin​−VH​)e−T/2τ
Vmin=VL+(Vmax−VL) e−T/2τV_{min} = V_L + (V_{max} - V_L)\,e^{-T/2\tau}Vmin​=VL​+(Vmax​−VL​)e−T/2τ
  • Rises for T/2 towards VH, falls for T/2 towards VL. Solve the pair.

2.1Worked examples

Exam values. Each one: what's new, the paper as printed, then the full solution.
Problem 2.1.1 (AUT22 · Q1(c), 20%). RC step up → capacitor voltage.
What's new here
  • Capacitor voltage can't jump: the start value is the old steady-state voltage.
  • Final value: C is a gap, so no current flows and e2 = the new source voltage.
  • Use t − t0 = 1 ms, not 2 ms.
Solution.
1.

Start value

Why Before the switch the capacitor was fully charged to V1 (no current, so no drop on R2). Capacitor voltage cannot jump.

e2(t0)=1 Ve_2(t_0) = 1\,\mathrm{V}e2​(t0​)=1V
2.

Final value

Why Given enough time the capacitor charges to the new source voltage.

e2(∞)=2 Ve_2(\infty) = 2\,\mathrm{V}e2​(∞)=2V
3.

Time constant

Why For RC, τ = R × C, with R the resistance the capacitor sees.

τ=R2C3=2200 Ω×470 nF=1.03 ms\tau = R_2C_3 = 2200\,\Omega\times470\,\mathrm{nF} = 1.03\,\mathrm{ms}τ=R2​C3​=2200Ω×470nF=1.03ms
4.

Time since the switch

Why The exponential starts at the switching instant, not at t = 0.

t−t0=2 ms−1 ms=1.00 mst - t_0 = 2\,\mathrm{ms} - 1\,\mathrm{ms} = 1.00\,\mathrm{ms}t−t0​=2ms−1ms=1.00ms
5.

Plug in

Why Start value, final value and τ are all you need.

x(t)=x∞+(x0−x∞) e−(t−t0)/τx(t) = x_\infty + (x_0 - x_\infty)\,e^{-(t-t_0)/\tau}x(t)=x∞​+(x0​−x∞​)e−(t−t0​)/τ
e2=2.00+(1.00−2.00) e−0.9671=1.62 Ve_2 = 2.00 + (1.00 - 2.00)\,e^{-0.9671} = \boxed{1.62\,\mathrm{V}}e2​=2.00+(1.00−2.00)e−0.9671=1.62V​
Trap Putting t = 2 ms straight into the exponential. The clock starts at t0 = 1 ms.
Paper issue The paper says "C1 is fully charged" but the capacitor in the figure is C3. It is a typo.
Answer.e2(t) = 1.62 V
Problem 2.1.2 (AUT23 · Q1(c), 20%). RL step from a non-zero start → node voltage.
What's new here
  • Non-zero start: V1 was 1 V for a long time, so the inductor already carries current.
  • Find the inductor current first (one loop, L = wire), then e3 = I·R4.
  • τ = L / (R2 + R4).
Solution.
1.

Current before the step

Why V1 was steady for a long time, so the inductor is a wire and the current is V/(R2+R4). Inductor current cannot jump, so this is also the start value.

i(t0)=1.00 VR2+R4=1.001000+1200=455 μAi(t_0) = \frac{1.00\,\mathrm{V}}{R_2 + R_4} = \frac{1.00}{1000+1200} = 455\,\mu\mathrm{A}i(t0​)=R2​+R4​1.00V​=1000+12001.00​=455μA
2.

Final current

Why Same idea with the new source voltage.

i(∞)=2.00 V1000+1200=909 μAi(\infty) = \frac{2.00\,\mathrm{V}}{1000+1200} = 909\,\mu\mathrm{A}i(∞)=1000+12002.00V​=909μA
3.

Time constant

Why Short V1: the inductor sees R2 and R4 in series.

τ=L3R2+R4=100 mH2200 Ω=45.5 μs\tau = \frac{L_3}{R_2+R_4} = \frac{100\,\mathrm{mH}}{2200\,\Omega} = 45.5\,\mu\mathrm{s}τ=R2​+R4​L3​​=2200Ω100mH​=45.5μs
4.

Plug in

Why Time since the step is t − t0 = 50.0 µs.

x(t)=x∞+(x0−x∞) e−(t−t0)/τx(t) = x_\infty + (x_0 - x_\infty)\,e^{-(t-t_0)/\tau}x(t)=x∞​+(x0​−x∞​)e−(t−t0​)/τ
i=909 μA+(455 μA−909 μA) e−1.100=758 μAi = 909\,\mu\mathrm{A} + (455\,\mu\mathrm{A} - 909\,\mu\mathrm{A})\,e^{-1.100} = 758\,\mu\mathrm{A}i=909μA+(455μA−909μA)e−1.100=758μA
5.

Node voltage

Why e3 is the voltage across R4.

e3=i R4=758 μA×1200 Ω=909 mVe_3 = i\,R_4 = 758\,\mu\mathrm{A}\times1200\,\Omega = \boxed{909\,\mathrm{mV}}e3​=iR4​=758μA×1200Ω=909mV​
Why it works AUT23 asked for e3 starting from 1 V. SPR24 asked for the current starting from 0 V. Same circuit, same method.
Answer.e3(t) = 909 mV
Problem 2.1.3 (SPR21 · Q1(c), 20%). Switch closes, inductor in parallel with a resistor.
What's new here
  • Start value given: I(L4) = 0.
  • Final: L4 is a wire, so e3 = 0. Node 3 has three branches → KCL.
  • τ: short V1, so R2 and R3 are in parallel.
✎ My notes

This is a tricky one. When L4 is a wire it puts e3 to 0, and then we use KCL to find the L4 current for x∞.

When I am looking for R, I need to short V1.

Solution.
1.

Start value

Why Inductor current cannot jump.

IL(0)=0I_{L}(0) = 0IL​(0)=0
2.

Final value

Why When settled, the inductor is a wire across R3. It shorts R3 out, so all of the current through R2 goes through the inductor.

IL(∞)=V1R2=1.002 V2000 Ω=501 μAI_L(\infty) = \frac{V_1}{R_2} = \frac{1.002\,\mathrm{V}}{2000\,\Omega} = 501\,\mu\mathrm{A}IL​(∞)=R2​V1​​=2000Ω1.002V​=501μA
3.

Resistance the inductor sees

Why Short V1. Looking out from the inductor, R2 and R3 both run from node 3 to ground, so they are in parallel.

Rth=R2∥R3=2000×30072000+3007=1.20 kΩR_{th} = R_2\parallel R_3 = \frac{2000\times3007}{2000+3007} = 1.20\,\mathrm{k}\OmegaRth​=R2​∥R3​=2000+30072000×3007​=1.20kΩ
4.

Time constant

Why τ = L / (Thévenin resistance seen by the inductor).

Problem 2.1.4 (SPR25 · Q1(b), 20%). Voltage pulse into RL → node voltage (sign trap).
What's new here
  • Pulse: two stages. Stage 2 starts from where stage 1 ended.
  • τ is the same in both stages.
  • Sign trap: after the pulse V1 = 0, so e2 = 0 − I·R1 is negative.
✎ My notes

The method for a pulse:

Stage 1: the normal formula, up to the end of the pulse.

The answer from stage 1 becomes the start of stage 2.

Stage 2: the normal formula again, heading to 0.

Solution.
1.

Time constant

Why R1, R2 and L are in series. The same τ applies while the pulse is on and after it ends.

τ=LR1+R2=100 mH1215 Ω=82.3 μs\tau = \frac{L}{R_1+R_2} = \frac{100\,\mathrm{mH}}{1215\,\Omega} = 82.3\,\mu\mathrm{s}τ=R1​+R2​L​=1215Ω100mH​=82.3μs
2.

Stage 1: pulse on (0 → 50.0 µs)

Why I starts at 0 and heads for V/(R1+R2). The pulse ends before it gets there.

I∞=V1R1+R2=2.001215=1.65 mAI_\infty = \frac{V_1}{R_1+R_2} = \frac{2.00}{1215} = 1.65\,\mathrm{mA}I∞​=R1​+R2​V1​​=12152.00​=1.65mA
I(tp)=I∞(1−e−tp/τ)=1.65 mA(1−e−0.6075)=749 μAI(t_p) = I_\infty\left(1 - e^{-t_p/\tau}\right) = 1.65\,\mathrm{mA}\left(1 - e^{-0.6075}\right) = 749\,\mu\mathrm{A}I(tp​)=I∞​(1−e−tp​/τ)=1.65mA(1−e−0.6075)=749μA
3.

Stage 2: pulse off

Why The source is now 0 V (a short). The current cannot jump, so it starts from I(tp) and decays towards 0.

I(t)=I(tp) e−(t−tp)/τ=749 μA×e−0.6075=408 μAI(t) = I(t_p)\,e^{-(t-t_p)/\tau} = 749\,\mu\mathrm{A}\times e^{-0.6075} = 408\,\mu\mathrm{A}I(t)=I(tp​)e−(t−tp​)/τ=749μA×e−0.6075=408μA
4.

Node 2

Why KVL from ground up through V1 and across R1. V1 is now 0 but the inductor keeps the current flowing, so node 2 goes negative.

e2=V1−IR1=0−408 μA×1200 Ω=−490 mVe_2 = V_1 - I R_1 = 0 - 408\,\mu\mathrm{A}\times1200\,\Omega = \boxed{-490\,\mathrm{mV}}e2​=V1​−IR1​=0−408μA×1200Ω=−490mV​
Trap Writing a positive answer. After the pulse, the inductor is the source and node 2 sits below ground.
Why it works AUT24 asked for I. SPR25 used the same circuit and asked for e2.
Answer.e2(t) = -490 mV
Problem 2.1.5 (AUT25 · Q3, 50 marks). Square wave into RC: steady-state max and min.
What's new here
  • Square wave, after the start-up has died away: it repeats every period.
  • High half: rises from Vmin towards VH. Low half: falls from Vmax towards VL. Each lasts T/2.
  • Two equations, two unknowns (Vmax, Vmin).
Solution.
1.

(b) · Period

Why A linear circuit driven by a periodic source settles to a waveform with the same period as the source.

T=1f=15 kHz=200 μsT = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{5\,\mathrm{kHz}} = \boxed{200\,\mu\mathrm{s}}T=f1​=5kHz1​=200μs​
2.

Time constant vs half period

Why T/2 is not much bigger than τ, so the capacitor never finishes charging or discharging. x is the fraction of the gap that is left after one half-cycle.

τ=RC=10 kΩ×22 nF=220 μs,T2=100 μs\tau = RC = 10\,\mathrm{k}\Omega\times22\,\mathrm{nF} = 220\,\mu\mathrm{s}, \qquad \frac{T}{2} = 100\,\mu\mathrm{s}τ=RC=10kΩ×22nF=220μs,2T​=100μs
x=e−(T/2)/τ=e−0.4545=0.6347x = e^{-(T/2)/\tau} = e^{-0.4545} = 0.6347x=e−(T/2)/τ=e−0.4545=0.6347
3.

Rising half (source high)

Why Start at Vmin, head for Vh. After T/2 the remaining gap has shrunk by the factor x.

Vmax=Vh−(Vh−Vmin) xV_{max} = V_h - (V_h - V_{min})\,xVmax​=Vh​−(Vh​−Vmin​)x
4.

Falling half (source low)

Why Start at Vmax, head for Vl. Same shrink factor.

Vmin=Vl+(Vmax−Vl) xV_{min} = V_l + (V_{max} - V_l)\,xVmin​=Vl​+(Vmax​−Vl​)x
5.

(c), (d) · Solve the pair

Why Substitute one equation into the other. The answers are symmetric about the middle of the square wave.

Vmax=Vl+Vh−Vl1+x=0+8.001+0.6347=4.89 VV_{max} = V_l + \frac{V_h - V_l}{1+x} = 0 + \frac{8.00}{1+0.6347} = \boxed{4.89\,\mathrm{V}}Vmax​=Vl​+1+xVh​−Vl​​=0+1+0.63478.00​=4.89V​
Vmin=Vl+(Vh−Vl) x1+x=3.11 VV_{min} = V_l + \frac{(V_h - V_l)\,x}{1+x} = \boxed{3.11\,\mathrm{V}}Vmin​=Vl​+1+x(Vh​−Vl​)x​=3.11V​
6.

(a) · Sketch

Why Low first half: Vc decays from Vmax to Vmin. High second half: it rises back to Vmax. Label both levels, T/2 and T.

Why it works Check: Vmax + Vmin = Vh + Vl = 8.00 V. The average of Vc equals the average of the square wave.
Answer.Period = 200 µs  ·  Vc,max = 4.89 V  ·  Vc,min = 3.11 V
